utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good morning, everybody. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Ms. Tapuskovic, Mr. Nikolic, and I think that's it. Prosecution is represented today by Mr. McCloskey. Do you think you will finish today, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And could I ask you, Mr. Ostojic, if you intend to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. We do for the time estimate 45 minutes to an hour, but I think Madam Nikolic may have direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm coming to Madam Nikolic. And Ms. Nikolic, do you still intend to examine this witness as your witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes. We will have some questions, and we need about four hours for those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. We indicated 20 minutes for cross-examination of this witness. I will stick to this estimation for the moment. I will have to wait for this witness to finish his examination-in-chief, and then we will make a final decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau yesterday indicated that she doesn't have any. And Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I indicated one hour, but I think we will have ten minutes, even that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Haynes? You had requested two hours initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That may be a little pessimistic. Maybe by about 100 per cent. I think we will probably be about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. So we know where we are, and your cross-examination as things stand at present, Mr. McCloskey? You had originally stated four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At present I don't have anywhere near four hours, but we will have to see, obviously, but at present, no. Nowhere near four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then we can start again, Mr. Zivanovic. Good morning, Colonel Vuga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic will proceed with his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, first of all let me ask you to clarify a term that you used yesterday. In many documents issued by the Army of Republika Srpska, the same term is mentioned. You said yesterday that the groups that launched attacks from the protected area were sabotage and terrorist units. From the point of view of military terminology and the terminology of the security organs, this term, "terrorist," is it justified; and if it is, why is it justified?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the selection of targets and by the consequences of attacks, the notion of terrorism implies sowing of terror among the population and in the environs. Any form of activity that produces such effects and attacks on facilities which are not purely military by nature have the characteristics of terrorist actions. If we are talking purely and exclusively about military facilities during combat between the warring parties when a cease-fire is not in effect, then we are talking about sabotage actions. The difference between the two lies in what I've just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask you to go back to point 4.25 in your report on page 38, and 46 in the English translation. The number of the document is 1D1075. And I'm referring you to item 4.25 in your report. The report is in the first binder, and the document that we will discuss is in the third binder. The report is in 1D1175, the report itself. Were you able to locate that document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you referred to this document, so I would kindly ask you to tell us briefly what the document is all about.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are on the same page, then we are talking about the term of corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we are not on the same page. Your report is item or chapter 4.25. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you provide more detail of the essence of your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find chapter 4.25 of your report? This is about a document dated 11 April 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an instruction if I'm now on the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: An instruction of the security organ of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, which refers to the arrest and bringing in prisoners of war and other persons. I studied the document from the point of view of security. The instruction that was sent to the security organs in the lower level units subordinated to the corps command refers to the purely professional matters that concern the apprehension and bringing in of persons in order to prevent the leak of information through these persons that they might have collected during their bringing in because some weaknesses had appeared in this part of the tasks of the officers who had identified the places of their collection and the directions of their escort. Those who were escorted were in a position to collect information that would have been of some interest for the side that they worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, does this document refer only to prisoners of war, or does it also refer to other persons who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document refers to anybody who was arrested and prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, in your report, you also speak about the obligations of Vujadin Popovic in relation to the operation that the Army of Republika Srpska was engaged in in Zepa. As a security organ, what were his obligations vis-a-vis an operation of that kind?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The obligations of the chief of the security staff of the Drina Corps as well as the assistant commander for security in Zepa operation were primarily to make sure that the system of command functioned safely. In other words, he was duty-bound to secure the command post from which the combat operation would be commanded, and he had to secure it in such a way as to not disrupt the system of command. He had to provide counter-intelligence security and organize measures of security within the command itself, such measures that would provide for the uninterrupted functioning of the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When such activities are carried out, providing security for the command post in such operations, when is that done and where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some critical points that must be controlled. The most critical point is the time of preparedness of the command post and putting it in function because it is at that very moment that the enemy tries to interfere, knowing that it is very complicated to start from scratch at the moment when combat is about to start. This is a very critical moment, and that's when all the security measures have to be in place and they have to start functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about Vujadin Popovic's duties, and I'm going to show you a number of documents dating back to 1995, ones that we came by at least. I don't think you have them in your binder, but you will be able to see them on the screen. When you do, could you please tell us whether such tasks fall under the purview of the security organ and into what groups of tasks that you spoke about during earlier days. Could we please now look at 1D1076. Did you have an occasion to see this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have an occasion to see this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether such tasks as indicated in this document fall within the purview of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document which belongs to the part of the professional guidance by the security organ along the counter-intelligence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D977?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, the interpreters have drawn our attention that you need to speak into the microphone as much as you can, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D977, please. I don't think we have a translation of this document yet, so could you just briefly explain to the Trial Chamber the nature of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document points to the fact that a person under a false identity was supposed to be found in Republika Srpska engaged in some activities, and his real identity did not match the documents. The obligation is the same -- similar if not the same as in the previous document. This is a counter-intelligence task in order to establish his whereabouts and what his activities were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 1D979? This is another document that has not been translated, so I would kindly ask you briefly what the document is about. Would you like to have it blown up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not necessary. I was reading, but it was not easy to recognise it. Now it's okay. This is another counter-intelligence document, and it refers to a report of the security organ. They are duty-bound to take measures to see how he was trying to persuade people to abandon the army and everything else that was behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is about --

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the troops of the Army of Republika Srpska are being persuaded to emigrate abroad, and it is not excluded that these are also counter-intelligence activities against the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D1288. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly about the nature of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The counter-intelligence work is aimed at looking at the activities of the American intelligence service and whether it is targeted at the Drina Corps and the commands subordinated to the Drina Corps. In other words, this document shows some of the counter-intelligence activities of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since the document has not been translated, can you just briefly tell us something about the nature of this document? What is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of this document points to the fact that the lorry drivers of the UNHCR in the territory of Republika Srpska were actually people who were engaged by the American intelligence service as is stated herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So this document expresses a doubt that these people were involved in intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about an obligation to establish that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D981. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say something about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very significant document for the security organs because the security organs had a long-term task according to this document, and that task was to engage in counter-intelligence and look at the volunteers arriving from the SRJ in order to discover among them those with different motives and intentions because their arrival did not always coincide with the interests and goals of the Army of Republika Srpska. That is why this had to be borne in mind, and their true goals and intentions could come to the fore at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D539.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, 1D539.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is in e-court. I found it in e-court. 1D539. I found it in e-court. It is on my display.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We can proceed, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, can you see this document? Can we zoom in a bit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you assist the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Vuga, I believe you saw in previous documents, and it's in this one as well; can you tell us to whom were all these documents sent by the security organ of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these documents were sent to chiefs of security organs of subordinated units. Let me not read the list. Units subordinated to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now look at this one, as well, and tell us, does this also fall within the scope of work of security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, but it doesn't fall within counter-intelligence. It falls within staff and command affairs because these affairs are conducted following orders down the chain of command, so there is an order. And pursuant to that order, security organs are to take the steps required here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this one is not translated yet, can you just tell us briefly what is required, what is demanded, by this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Measures were required to be taken to protect the secrecy of places and areas where UNPROFOR members who were arrested were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now move to 1D983?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we at least find out who sent that document, what date it was? I mean, I couldn't tell from that. I mean, this series of -- we are completely in the dark on this but a few basics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you give us that information, Mr. Zivanovic, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All of these documents were sent by security chief of Drina Corps, Mr. Vujadin Popovic. It is a whole series of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I couldn't make the date out, and the time period of taking UN prisoners is of interest. I can recognise some words in here, but I won't say which words I can recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then come back to the previous document, 539, and you will tell us, Mr. Vuga, about the date.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the document anymore, but it was the 23rd of June. Yes, it's back now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not the document we have just seen on the screen. The previous one.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous one was sent on the 31st of May, 1995. It was sent by the security section of the command of the Drina Corps. At that time, it was Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. I said earlier it was sent to the security organs of the units subordinated to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that will suffice. Can we now move on to 1D983? Are you able to tell us, first of all, are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It refers to preventing leaks in radio traffic, and discipline is required in radio traffic. The attention of security organs is drawn to the fact that they should monitor this problem with the means that they have at their disposal. That includes counter-intelligence, finding how and why; but also within the purview of command and staff affairs down the chain of command this problem is to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If there is anything mentioning the change of frequencies in this document, could it be read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. I can't help either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have a translation for this, could you read it and tell us -- I am sorry, I just see -- I just saw that this document was translated but it's filed under 3D319. 3D319 is the translation. So maybe we don't need to read it. The whole 3D319 can be shown because it was found on two lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That's a transcript. 3D.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D319.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If there is some mention of frequencies in this paragraph. I think it's short. If it's there, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, what is the heading in this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Discipline In Radio Communications, Observations." This document was drafted based on observations made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing I want to know, is the security of radio communications part of the responsibilities of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prevention of leaks of information is the job of security organs, regardless of how these leaks occur. In this case, we are dealing with leaks through radio traffic and radio communications intercepted by the enemy and the enemy's ability to do that. It refers to using devices for data protection and more frequent changes of frequencies so that communications cannot be listened to if they are being listened to on one frequency. If various frequencies are used, the enemy will get one part of the message but not all of it. The security organs are required to do whatever the regulations require them to do to prevent leaks in radio traffic whenever they have information that such leaks can occur and they can respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We've heard here that the VRS had various types of equipment for protecting radio communications, radio relay communications, et cetera. Can we see from this document which particular types of equipment are referred to? If you can see that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the devices is mentioned here, S-35, for cryptographic data protection. I've already said something about the degree to which it is necessary to protect a particular document. The information within a document is protected in such a way that for as long as this document is topical, premature leaking is prevented. Information that is leaked once it is no longer topical is not so significant. In fact, it has a historical significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is this document about? Does it also fall within the purview of security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does fall within the scope of work of security organs because the topic of this document - that is activities - was a subject of abuse and problems in these communications that were maintained in the area of the Drina Corps through sponsorship, but also on the territory where sponsors were active in locations where it was not desirable and there was the possibility of abuse of this sponsorship. Counter-intelligence work is called for here to see what was going on without disturbing regular forms of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, could you just look at one more document, 1D990. Do you recall this document? Was it within the scope of work of security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. It has two dimensions. The Main Staff ordered how to treat journalists and reporters. Security organs had an obligation as counter-intelligence agents in the area of the corps to keep this kind of work under control, as well, and to have full information about what is going on; but we see also from this document that this order was not consistently executed, so the security organs are reminded once again to activate measures of protection and to warn journalists and reporters that they may not visit without a special permission from the Main Staff. It falls within command and staff affairs but also within the area of counter-intelligence protection of sensitive spots.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe on the first day of your testimony one document of the BH army was mentioned ordering general mobilisation of all men of military age. Can you tell us if you have ever seen a document after -- saying that after the demilitarisation and the proclamation of Srebrenica as an UNPA there occurred a demobilisation of men living in those territories?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall if I found a single line of text written about that. No, not a single word or a single line about demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We know -- I mean, you certainly had seen documents related to the column that started moving from Srebrenica towards the territory held by the BH army. Can you tell us whether there were also unarmed men of military age in that column?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were also unarmed men of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you know, what was the reason for that decision to include in the column unarmed men of military age alongside members of the 28th Division? Have you seen any documents or any other information that could explain this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a decision communicated in one of the documents to form this column provided with armed escort so that they could go through the territory controlled by Serb forces and reach or rather break through to the territory held by Muslim forces. Military experience and military knowledge tells us that there is no army that can relinquish or sacrifice so easily a whole division with all its equipment. A division with all its equipment is a formidable force, a very necessary one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the documents that you analysed, were you able to find out what was happening with those people in that column who ended up in the territory held by the BH army after the 16th and the 17th of July, 1995, and later?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make my answer very brief, there are several documents, and one of them speaks explicitly about how they were received and the kind of units that were organised from the 28th Division, how volunteers were recruited among them to go back to the territory they came from so that they could be infiltrated and help those who had not yet managed to break through to the territory held by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now see document 1D1280. 1D1280. It's the wrong document, I'm sorry. Can we look at 1281? This one is wrong too. I apologise. We are not going to show documents any more. Could we go back now to the 12th of July, 1995. From the documents that we have, we know that at that time Vujadin Popovic was seen in Bratunac and in Potocari. Since you know what was going on in Potocari at that time, tell us whether his presence in those locations was justified from the viewpoint of his regular duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This assumes the fact that not in evidence that this man knows what was going on in Potocari at the time. Perhaps a foundational question would be, you know, what based on your view of whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, fair enough. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very good point. I'll ask it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, do you know what was going on on the 12th of July, 1995, in Potocari? Have you seen that from the documents you studied?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did analyse documents dealing with the developments in Potocari on the 12th, and these documents speak of large number of people who found themselves in Potocari, either in the UN base or around it, or should I say UN forces located in Srebrenica. That was a very variegated group, a large mass of people that was awaiting a denouement of all these events. Since it was the territory of the Drina Corps, the security organ and the military police acting pursuant to regulations had the obligation to gain an insight into all these developments to prevent a possible surprise because there was no control yet over this large mass of people, and anything could be expected to originate from that large group of people that would endanger security. High-risk situations in general incorporating such a large component of security risk require the presence of a security organ who would be able to quickly evaluate the situation and select the best response from his own area of work as well as provide adequate information to others who would take adequate steps within their respective scope of work. That was the role of Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To clarify what you just said, you said there was a large number of people in the UN base and outside the base. Can you tell us more closely who these people were, at least their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. I don't see why this is relevant for there witness to tell us what we have been hearing for over a year now, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he testified on this, also, yesterday with reference to a particular document that Mr. Zivanovic showed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's true, but Mr. McCloskey asked for foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, can you now tell me this: You spoke about this yesterday, and you said that amongst other things there are also documents showing that there were also BiH army soldiers among the refugees in Potocari. According to the rules that were in force at the time, was there a legal foundation to separate those for whom there was a suspicion that they were members of the armed forces of the enemy from the group of refugees?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regulation on the service of the military police and the instruction on the use of the military police provide for the military police to check refugees and to try and discover those persons who merged with the refugees in order to hide their identity and to move together with the refugees most commonly to the side that will guarantee them safety as they see fit. Second of all, the security organ is duty-bound in those terms to establish whether that process from the point of view of the profession evolves in a proper manner and on the other hand to take over such persons for whom it has been established under the regulations that the military police should hand them over to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the military police hands over persons to the security organ, do we know who these persons are? Could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is provided for by regulations, which say that any crime that might have been committed by these persons and which fall within the purview of the security organs' duties, they have to be handed over to the security organ. Everything else, everybody else, will be prisoners of war which will be checked once the conditions for that are in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Persons who are separated in this way from the group of civilians, will they have their freedom of movement and communication limited? Do the regulations allow for these persons' freedom of movement and communication to be limited, that they be separated from the rest of the group?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the criteria that are envisaged, the separating people from the group represents the limitation of their freedoms of movement and communication. As soon as they were separated, these people were placed under the so-called isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would this be similar to an arrest?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is identical to an arrest. However, when a person is arrested, you know in advance the reason for which the person is arrested, whereas in this particular case, the -- all the actions that are necessary to establish that should follow after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at Prosecutor's document number 242. Are you familiar the document? Can you see it all right on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us the nature of this document. What is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a list of 387 names of persons for whom there is a suspicion that they committed war crimes and who were supposed to be identified in the place where identification was being carried out, in all such places. This was the obligation of all those who were involved in identifications, primarily the MP, because military police are charged with identification of people as well as all those who had other duties when recording the names of the people in such places where conditions for that were in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now move to the last page of the document just to look at the date when it was drafted. You will find the date at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is 12 July 1995 in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, you have already told us something about Zepa operation. Did you come by information as to what had happened with the units that participated in Krivaja 95 once Srebrenica was taken? Do you know what happened to them after that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once Srebrenica was taken, both units had participated in Krivaja 95, so those units were redirected to another task, which was to take Zepa following an order that ensued after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the order by the Supreme Commander to disarm all Muslim terrorist gangs? I believe that's the precise word that was used in this document dated 9 July. We've already spoken about it, and if you want to do that, we can look at it again. Does this mean that these units were not sent into that operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that they were redirected to Zepa confirms the fact that they did not continue any activities regarding the disarming of the Muslim forces that had left Srebrenica by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now can we look at Prosecutor's Exhibit number 131. I believe you have it in your binder.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, who was it who sent this document and who signed it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant commander, Major General Zdravko Tolimir, and the date on the document is 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I now ask you, please, to look at the time when the document was dispatched?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time is 2230 hours. This is when the document was dispatched, on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was Mr. Tolimir's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Zdravko Tolimir was the assistant commander of the Main Staff for security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us the outlines of this document. What is it that Mr. Tolimir indicates in this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is information or information about the fact that in Sjemec in the facilities of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, there are accommodations for 800 prisoners of war, and it says further on if there is not enough room for them to be accommodated, they could be accommodated in Sjemec where they could be engaged in farm work. They would tend to horses, pigs, and sheep. In other words, they would be involved in the farming activities as stated herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, in this courtroom we heard that the Army of Republika Srpska when planning and executing the Krivaja 95 operation had a predesigned plan to kill all able-bodied Muslims that would be arrested or that would surrender to them. Could you please tell me whether you came by any document demonstrating that before the 13th of July, 1995, any such plan existed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, after the analysis of all the documents that were studied from the point of view of security, one could get a grasp of their main contents and see whether the security aspect of these documents point to a possibility that prisoners of war might be killed contrary to the Geneva Conventions and the customs of war under international documents and the laws of Republika Srpska. The documents that I studied contain quite a number of orders to the units and officers engaged in Krivaja 95, ordering them to strictly comply with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. The president, moreover, orders a step further, which is to make sure that civilian facilities were not destructed unless it was so required by military goals. In other words, I did not come by anything that would point to the fact that there might be an instance of killing of prisoners of war from the point of view of planning and execution of the Krivaja 95 operation before the date that you indicated and asked me whether there was anything to such an effect in the documents issued before the 13th of July, 1995, i.e. before the time indicated on the document that is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of the list that you looked at, does this list tell you that at the time no such plan was in place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It is leading, Mr. Zivanovic. If you could rephrase it, although I think it's too late now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, what was the purpose of drafting a list of potential prisoners of war in this particular situation that we have just spoken about as it was on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of compiling a list of war crime suspects was to place them under a special treatment because they were in for a procedure that would establish exactly whether they are liable or not according to the rules of Republika Srpska and international conventions regarding the separation of persons that might be subject to further processing. In order for them to be separated from the rest of the group, such a list had to be compiled. And that was its main purpose, to separate such potential suspects from those who did not fall under that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that there should have been a different treatment between war crime suspects and others?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, this is contained in my previous answer. As soon as they are separated, that means that they would be processed, and let me put it this way: This was a more strict form of isolation aimed at making sure that these persons would not become subject of exchange or anything else because they were potentially criminally liable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Within that context, how do you look at the letter that you see on the screen sent by General Tolimir, the list that contains his proposal for a certain number of prisoners of war to be accommodated in the facilities indicated in the letter?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mere fact that a certain number of prisoners of war will be involved in farm works according to this letter points to the fact that they would be treated in a different way in view of the fact that they were not on the list, so they could enjoy the status of prisoners of war rather than of persons that are in for a criminal procedure pending against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the chain or in the hierarchy of the Republika Srpska army, was it possible to create a plan about killing of all able-bodied men who were either arrested or who surrendered themselves without a person in the position of General Zdravko Tolimir being aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel Zivanovic please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By his position -- by virtue of his position, General Tolimir had to be informed about everything that was going on in the Army of Republika Srpska and particularly when it came to the activities surrounding Krivaja 1995, which is confirmed by this document. In other words, he's speaking about prisoners of war that the President of the republic ordered to be disarmed, and also he said that all those who had participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska should be treated as prisoners of war. In other words, General Tolimir must have been aware of what was going on. If not, he could not have issued such information because it would have been pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question was not interpreted in full because I said part of it while not speaking into the microphone. I will restate that part of the question, and you will either leave your answer as it is or answer differently. So my question is: Was it possible to have a plan to kill all able-bodied men who surrendered or who had been captured without a person like General Zdravko Tolimir in the position that he held knowing anything about it at the time when he sent this letter?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a question phrased like that, I can answer that it would have been possible only if General Tolimir had been completely left out of the loop as far as this plan is concerned. General Tolimir as a member of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska would have been otherwise involved in that plan. He would have had to execute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for him in his position to know nothing about such a plan?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- I said he was assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs. By virtue of his position, he would have been the best-informed man in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me something else. From the document you had occasion to analyse, what happened later on that 13th of July, 1995? Do you know what happened with the column that was moving from Srebrenica towards the territory held by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column that had been formed and was escorted or was breaking out under arms came into the area of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. They launched a breakout, and from the documents I analysed that disposition was such that it really had the nature of a breakout from encirclement, and that is the main feature of that stage of entry of the column into the area of the Zvornik Brigade because the whole territory they were breaking out of was under the control of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, was any decision made regarding prisoners? Did you come across or analyse one of the documents of the Drina Corps command or, more precisely, the Drina Corps commander from that time? Could we look at P36, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, could we get more precise on what day? I mean, it's not exactly clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is omitted obviously. It was the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really need a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the break. Would 25 minutes be enough for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it will be enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, before continuing with my questions, over the break we realised that you seemed to be tired. If that is indeed the case, please say so, and then the Chamber may discuss any possibilities in relation to that. Please tell us if you are extremely tired.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chamber gave me the choice to decide how far I can go. When going through the testimony in my head, I realised that I may have caused some damage in terms of providing the answers which are not the best, but I will do my utmost to keep it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because this is a statement that doesn't really make me feel serene, and serenity of mind is perhaps one of the most important requisites for good judgement on our part on a daily basis. Are you in a position to continue? If you have a preference, if you think that you shouldn't continue, that we should give you a complete rest today, then I can assure you we will find absolutely no difficulty at all, Colonel. We are not here to make it difficult for anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understood you well. It was my mistake that at a certain point - however, it wasn't today but yesterday - I didn't provide the best of explanations and I couldn't go at full thrust, but I feel all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Then let's continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, previously, when you were talking about the documents you analysed, you mentioned what was taking place with unarmed military-age men who left Srebrenica in the column and found themselves in the territory that was controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I tried showing you some documents. However, I made an error, but now I have the right figures, the right numbers, and I want to show them to you, and perhaps then you can tell us whether these were the documents you had in mind. That is 1D1080.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the English version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you will be able to see it now in the B/C/S original. Is that one of the documents, Mr. Vuga?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. There is also a document of the 28th of July in the form of a report pertaining to the 27th of July from the 2nd Corps command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which states that the 2nd Corps command had registered 2.311 fighters, members of the 28th Division, who were assigned to different units, and they were undergoing training and being rearmed in order to re-establish that unit again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us move to 1D1081 next. I believe that is the document you have in mind. [In English] Scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document I mentioned. This is a report which indicates the exact figures of those members who arrived per units. That is the report I had in mind. There is other data, but this data is closest in terms of being nearest to the date concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to where we left it off before the break. I asked you whether you know of the existence of an order of the Drina Corps command concerning the 13th of July, 1995, which referred or may have referred to POWs. Could we please look at P36 next.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the order before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us briefly what did you conclude from this order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps command on the 13th of July, 1995, as very urgent sent this order to the commands of all subordinate units of the Drina Corps, as well as to the forward command post of the Drina Corps for information so that they could carry out their tasks in relation to the issue concerned. The document states, "Blocking the passage of Muslim groups to Tuzla and Kladanj. Order." My attention was drawn to the first item of the order just below the heading. I just wanted to say that this obliged all the units. They were being informed that military-aged men from the enclave were tasked to divide themselves into groups and with arms to go in the direction of Tuzla and Kladanj. It reads further that among those, there are those who are criminals and villains who will stop at nothing to avoid being captured, and they will try to reach the territory that was under the control of the Muslims. This was a warning which stated that in addition to some armed and unarmed military-aged men who were supposed to be disarmed, all those involved will have to deal with those from the column who are qualified as such in the document. The idea behind this document warned those who were supposed to implement those tasks to be cautious so as to avoid any surprises and losses due to being careless and poorly informed in terms of what the enemy concerned was like. That is important because each commanding officer issuing an order is duty-bound to provide sufficient information that will provide for a successful implementation of the task or order involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 1 of the order -- well, based on that, can you tell us who the order was sent to and who was supposed to implement it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I read at the beginning, it was sent to the commands of all subordinate units and the IKM for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second item of the order is interesting in its part which says that all those who can carry weapons should be engaged. How do you interpret this part of the order? I have referred to only one part of the item. Perhaps I should have read out the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear from what you've said that this was a full mobilisation of all those who were able to participate in combat, i.e. to participate in the execution of the task as formulated therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 3 of the order, it is specified what needs to be done with those who are captured and disarmed. I won't go through the document item by item, but I wanted to ask you this: In this order, did you see a separate task assigned to the security organ in relation to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this order, there is no task requiring the attention of security organs. Their participation as part of this task was such that they carried out their own tasks as envisaged by the scope of activity and responsibilities of security organs. This only had to do with the security organs in cases that they have operational possibilities to provide information to the organs of the command and those implementing this task on the whereabouts of those groups and how one can secure as much information as possible on that groups. That was the task of the security organ because it had to do with the territory controlled by the VRS. In that territory, there was a security regimen in place ordered by the relevant commanders who were supposed to deal with the issues of security within their different areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Analysing these documents, did you come to learn what was happening with the column on that very day, the 13th of July, 1995, beginning with the evening hours or, rather, afternoon hours onwards? I'm talking about the 28th Division column, which was pulling out of Srebrenica. Could we please have a look at 1D965. Let us have a look at the front -- first page to be able to see what the document involved is. Mr. Vuga, did you have occasion to analyse this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I analysed certain parts of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the translation has not arrived yet. Can you tell us, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given that it's so short and it's dated 27 July, the question was about 13 July. Perhaps Mr. Zivanovic could just read this because I've just been in the dark on about 12 documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Fair enough. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We may move to page 4? [Interpretation] We can go to the bottom of the page. There is a paragraph -- I've just been informed that we do have a translation. It is 5D355.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 3D355.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the 13th of July, 1995, in particular the second part of the document, which begins with 1930 hours. I believe it's on the next page of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that in B/C/S in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, in the English translation, it is page 6. It begins with the paragraph beginning with, "At 7.30 p.m. " Could you please clarify for us what this concerns and whether you analysed this part of the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did analyse it from the point of view of consequences and the security situation. It was interesting because it pointed to a real possibility of an attack on Zvornik with the aim of stretching out the forces of the VRS and the Zvornik Brigade that were in control of the terrain to make it easier for the column to more easily reach the territory along the route they had envisaged. One -- among one of the things that were carried out was to construct false communication networks that were supposed to give an impression that there were other units - in fact, non-existent - which posed a threat to Zvornik. It was done in such a way that the various commands and intelligence organs of the VRS should be given wrong information that would make them conclude that the attack might be real.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just clarify this last bit in the passage, I quote, "especially when the action of NORA was incorporated against Zvornik." What is NORA?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an artillery weapon, and it was named when it was designed, a new piece of rocket artillery. This confirms what I said earlier. This was designed to create a convincing piece of disinformation so convincing that nobody could ignore it, that they had to take measures of defence depending on how great they evaluated the danger to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how did the VRS react to this threat to Zvornik? Were you able to see that from the documents?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was able to see how the VRS reacted, and that confirmed that this piece of disinformation was convincing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at document P165. Did you take this document into account? What does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an interim report on electronic reconnaissance. It comes from the command of the Drina Corps, the 4th radio reconnaissance platoon, and you see in the heading that it was provided to the intelligence administration of the Main Staff of the VRS, to the intelligence section of the Drina Corps, to the forward command post, that is to the commander personally, to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, and to the Birac Infantry Brigade. The document speaks about forces coming from Tuzla, forces of the BH Army coming from the Tuzla sector, headed by Naser Oric. It says they came across our forces in the Planinci sector, and it says that Naser Oric is boasting of all that he had achieved in that area. Let me not go into detail. The document speaks for itself. It says their aim is to create -- to wreak havoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D698, please. Did you analyse this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It's a document from the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What does it say, briefly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it refers to an evaluation made regarding the level of threat in the area covered by the Drina Corps and a demand to mobilise non-assigned conscripts to prevent the infiltration of sabotage terrorist forces and previously crushed Muslim forces from Srebrenica. It seems from the document that the situation in the area of the Drina Corps had become extremely complex since it was necessary to carry out a mobilisation to restore security to the level necessary for the execution of tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 1D651. Have you had occasion to see this document? What is it about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it. This document is a report on Muslim units. It says, "Intelligence has been collected through electronic surveillance that Naser Oric had made a breakout." We have seen that from the previous document, that he had reached the Krizevici sector, that he was going to Planinci in order to link up with a group from Srebrenica in order to wreak havoc in Zvornik. So it's very specific as to their intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next paragraph reads, "I have ordered complete mobilisation in Zvornik and that everyone be sent to positions for defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think this is for sure a one-page document, and I recognise the name Vinko down there. Could we have him read this so we can be in tune with what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who is going to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just informed that we have a translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, which is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Don't want to be suspicious, but I would hope that we could have English documents if they are up there. It seems they come up whenever I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, from my position here, I can see that Mr. Zivanovic was blissfully unaware of the existence of the translations and that he is being fed the information from some of his colleagues, so I don't have any -- I don't share any suspicions in his regard. But, again, you've done a wonderful job, Mr. Zivanovic. You've been very prepared. You have caused us very little problems, but this could have been averted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we haven't got the information that the document was translated under our exhibit number. This is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, I mean, I would assume that you submitted the same document to the CLSS for translation, and one of the things that we have been trying to avoid all along is duplicating the work of the CLSS staff, which are already inundated with work. But anyway, let's move, not waste more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you came in your answer to this point about general mobilisation in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that everyone should be mobilised and sent to positions. We see how seriously this was taken on the basis of intelligence collected, and it is suggested that Pandurevic and Legenda return to their zones to take measures to redress the consequences, if any, and to prevent catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at two more documents on the subject, 1D1291. Can you tell us, did you take this document into account as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And very briefly, it's a response to the demand of the Drina Corps command from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, which is acting upon the request cited earlier concerning mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This situation in Zvornik that you described that began in the evening of the 13th until this mobilisation, did it require the presence of the security organ of the Drina Corps in that territory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information that we have discussed so far and the procedure that was ordered in relation to the defence of Zvornik, the mobilisation that was to be carried out, and from these words, "to prevent a catastrophe," we see that all this needed to be done with maximum security measures; otherwise, it would indeed have caused a catastrophe to the defence of Zvornik, and we see that from the response of this organ that demanded the return of Pandurevic and Legenda. So in view of the responsibility of the command of the Drina Corps for mobilisation on its territory and in keeping with the rule on mobilisation, security organ of the Drina Corps had the obligation to take any measures within its jurisdiction to provide counter-intelligence support for this mobilisation, which was extremely important at that moment. He was alone, as we had occasion to note, and he could only do that by going to Zvornik because it was in Zvornik, in fact, that the whole situation had repercussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have looked at all the rules governing the work of security organs, and in your report you mention the rule on mobilisation, which is 1D5693. Tell us, does this rule prescribe such obligations and duties for the security organ, and if it does, what are these obligations exactly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I stated precisely what the responsibilities of the security organ are pursuant to the rule on mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Drop the 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has not been translated yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But still, could you tell us very briefly, does this document envisage any obligations for the security organ in relation to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, but it's in another passage. The heading says, "Support of mobilisation." There are various sorts of support to mobilisation, various types. There are several.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to the following page, please? The same document. Can you now tell us, which part of this document prescribes the duties of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, the security support. This is where the security support issues are regulated, and on the right-hand side, in this area here, and I can't see the page number, under 321, it says -- bullet point 3, where it says, "Measures for the timely discovery and prevention of intelligence, reconnaissance, sabotage, and other subversive activities of the internal and external enemy targeted and aimed at jeopardising preparations and execution of mobilisation." In this particular case, it is all about the execution of mobilisation because mobilisation had been ordered with an immediate effect. Further on, under 322 a reference is made to the counter-intelligence evaluation, and we've already spoken about the measures contained therein. In this particular case, it should have applied to the immediate situation in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, was it possible during this period of time that we are talking about for these duties and tasks in -- not to be performed by anybody in the corps if Vujadin Popovic was not available to perform them? Is it possible that during this period of time there was nobody to attend to these duties, so they would not be carried out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The importance of the duties of the security organ and the importance of mobilisation as an action, of importance for combat, provide for those actions to be carried out in very secure conditions. The mobilisation activity is of critical importance under the conditions that prevailed at the time, and putting mobilisation in jeopardy would jeopardise the whole of the defence given the conditions. In other words, it should not have been allowed for mobilisation to fail for one reason or another and especially for the reasons of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to have just a few more questions for you, but tell me, please, if you're in any way indisposed, tired, or --

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's continue. Put your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the security tasks cannot be transferred to anyone else when we are talking about the rules governing the work of the security organ, the regulations, and all the other instructions. What about the tasks relative to mobilisation? Could those duties of the security organ be transferred to somebody else or, to put it in more simple terms, could Vujadin Popovic have charged somebody else with mobilisation issues?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I said that no authorities could be transferred to other people because those were personal, and there was a document proving that that was the case, and I'm talking about the official ID of the security organ. What stands behind all this is the following: The part concerning the counter-intelligence evaluation, the collection of information by applying the methods of work of the security organ, is absolutely non-transferrable, and it is within the exclusive purview of the persons vested with the relevant authorities. This would be my answer or part of my answer, and the answer is that what Colonel Vujadin Popovic was supposed to do in Zvornik could not have been done by anybody else in view of the prevalent situation at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the last thing I wanted to ask you about is this: When analysing all the documents, did you come by any documents showing how it all ended with the column? How did the whole column situation end? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the end of the situation with the column, there are documents reaching up to the month of September that speak of the instances of groups of people appearing or individuals who had been in the column and who were still trying to reach the territory under the control of the Muslim side. They appeared in the area where the column had been broken up. I'm not able to precisely define when the whole thing ended because in my view a threat to security by its intensity and by everything that happened ended earlier in terms of my conclusions. This happened subsequently, after the critical events that we are talking about, after the execution of prisoners of war, where it was carried out, and the rest was dealt with successively as could be done by the forces controlling the territory. When they came in contact with the remains of that column, they would take them prisoners. That's my end to your question as to how this ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that my question was not very precise. Let me rephrase the question and ask you, do you know what happened when the main body of the column that was trying to break through from Srebrenica to the territory under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Now I have been redirected in more precise terms, and I can tell you this. A corridor was opened to let through the unarmed persons from the column into the Muslim territory, and this happened on the 16th of July. This corridor functioned up to the 17th. There is information to that effect on the Muslim side about the passage and reception of these persons among whom there were also unarmed members of the 28th Division. Later on, they were registered in the list that we saw just a little while ago, and we saw how they were treated subsequently. That is as far as the column is concerned or at least that part of the column that was in the corridor and that was let through during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information according to which Vujadin Popovic received a number of tasks, among which to go and report on the events that happened on the day when the corridor was opened. My question to you is this: Can you tell us whether such a task would be in keeping with the function that he discharged and the other tasks that he had?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the purview of the security organ's duties and in view of the situation that prevailed at the time when these events were taking place, there is a very important fact that I would like to convey and share with you so that you may be able to understand what I'm talking about, and I'll try and be brief. Based on experience, the territory of the Zvornik Brigade had been used to move arms into Srebrenica. The length of that line at the moment was about 80 kilometres. That's where the group infiltrated with the arms for Srebrenica being --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Colonel. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This was a very specific question. If we could get the answer and then the explanation just because that's the appropriate procedure, and this is going to be a continuing issue, obviously, as we have additional questioning by additional counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, we appreciate the big efforts that you are making in trying to answer the questions and trying to give as much information as you can. On the other hand, the practice here is to stick to the question as much as possible and resort to explanations and further details only if necessary, considered necessary by you, and normally you would ask us to go beyond what you're being asked or to explain your answer. In this case, I suggest that you answer the question and you continue to explain precisely why your answer is what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just reaching the end of my explanation, but it doesn't really matter. I'll answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, then. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how things stand. There was a great deal of risk in the corridor where it was opened because the corridor also functioned during the night. If any -- there was a -- quite a likelihood for a group to pass through in an opposite direction and bring arms to those who were not able to break through. And that would have created a huge problem in depth, and I provided my explanation to show what the basis was for that evaluation that had to be taken into account and that had to be acted upon urgently and without any delays.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the rules and tasks of the security organ, what degree of presence and what length of presence on the part of Vujadin Popovic was requested in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm talking about does not have any temporal limitations. This is the issue of a situation that cannot be put in any specific terms. A lot of time lapsed, and a lot of the circumstances that prevailed at the time and that had to be taken into account can no longer be assessed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of his tasks, was it indispensable for Popovic to be there until the moment the corridor was finally closed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Colonel. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is vague. Where? And what time period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The time period I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've seen this witness go off and try to answer his own questions based on imprecise questions, and that's what's going to happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The question is not imprecise because if Mr. McCloskey followed the answer of the witness, he told us that the corridor was opened on 16th July and closed on 17 July. It was the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Time-wise, I think you are right. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've just left, I believe, Colonel Popovic at the IKM. Is that where we are, or are we somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He spoke about IKM. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where did he have to be according to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was should he be -- if he had to be at the Baljkovica when the corridor was closed? It was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then answer -- that's more simple, and the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My simplest answer would be yes, and I've already provided ample elements to show why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question for you, Mr. Vuga: In the overall analysis of the documents that you analysed, did you come across any sort of participation of Vujadin Popovic in the execution of the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I was very concrete. In terms of my attitude towards documents, in operative and combat documents that I analysed, I did not come across the role of -- or participation of Vujadin Popovic in the execution of the prisoners of war. There are witness statements that I analysed and provided my opinion about, but no witness statements could help me to arrive at a reliable conclusion or help me to form an opinion that would be unambiguous as to the role of Vujadin Popovic in this act of execution, and this would be my answer based on what I put in my report, and I adhere by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vuga. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have finished my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Ms. Nikolic, do you wish to start now, or do you wish to break now? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this would be a very good moment for a break. It would allow me to organise my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel, I understand you wish to address the Trial Chamber. Do I have the right information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say, Your Honour, that the work so far and everything that has happened so far has made an impact on my situation that you're aware of, and a break until tomorrow would allow me to recover and be better suited to continue working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. By all means, Colonel. We fully understand, and you will find us cooperative. So you can withdraw, and if you're feeling all right, then we continue, we resume, tomorrow morning at 9.00, and take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Your Honour, and I shall do my best certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, it's not over yet. Now, yesterday, we had a short discussion, us and Mr. Ostojic and Mr. McCloskey, on pending matters arising in the wake of the various Beara motions.
